items.title: Dictionary definition of 'ancient' (Cambridge UK)
items.body: The Cambridge UK dictionary defines "ancient" as an adjective meaning of or from a long time ago, having lasted for a very long time, or very old. topic.summary: The Cotswolds is an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty in England designated in August 1966 and now presented as a National Landscape. topic.intro: The Cotswolds AONB is one of 34 protected landscapes in England. Designated in the mid-1960s, it is managed as a National Landscape following the 2023 rebranding, while retaining its statutory AONB status.

The dataset is maintained by Natural England and provides the official designation chronology for English AONBs.

items.title: Protected under Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000

topic.title: Cotswold Region Tourism
topic.summary: The Cotswolds is a National Landscape in south-central England covering nearly 800 square miles across six counties, known for honey-coloured stone villages, rolling hills, and historic market towns.
topic.intro: Designated an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty in 1966 (now a National Landscape), the Cotswolds attracts millions of visitors yearly with its Jurassic limestone geology, medieval wool-trade heritage, and quintessentially English countryside.

items.title: Area and Size
items.body: The Cotswolds covers nearly 800 square miles (2,038 km²) of south-central England, making it the largest designated landscape area in England and Wales. The region stretches across a broad swathe of countryside centred on the Cotswold escarpment, a ridge of Jurassic limestone hills.

items.title: National Landscape Designation
items.body: Originally designated an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty in 1966, the Cotswolds is now classified as a National Landscape. This status protects the region's distinctive character — golden stone villages, rolling hills, and ancient meadows — from inappropriate development.

items.title: Six Counties
items.body: The Cotswolds spans six English counties: Gloucestershire, Oxfordshire, Warwickshire, Wiltshire, Worcestershire, and Somerset. The heart of the region lies in Gloucestershire and Oxfordshire, with the northern edge reaching Warwickshire and the southern edge touching Somerset.

items.title: Jurassic Limestone Geology
items.body: The region's distinctive golden stone comes from Jurassic oolitic limestone, quarried since Roman times. This geology creates the Cotswolds' trademark warm yellow buildings, dry-stone walls, gently folded valleys, and springy wildflower meadows that define the landscape.

items.title: Cotswold Way Trail
items.body: The 102-mile Cotswold Way is a popular long-distance walking trail running from Chipping Campden to Bath. It passes through some of the region's most scenic spots, including classic villages and historic market towns, offering walkers a comprehensive Cotswolds experience.

items.title: Name Etymology
items.body: The name 'Cotswolds' derives from Old English: 'cot' meaning sheep enclosure and 'wold' meaning rolling hillsides. This reflects the region's origins as a pastoral area where sheep farming generated medieval wealth that funded the grand churches and manor houses still standing today.

items.title: Famous Villages
items.body: Iconic Cotswolds villages include Bourton-on-the-Water (called the 'Venice of the Cotswolds' for its stone bridges over the River Windrush), Bibury with its 17th-century Arlington Row weavers' cottages, Castle Combe, and Lacock, which have featured in period dramas and films.

items.title: Location Relative to Cities
items.body: The Cotswolds sits in south-central England between Oxford to the east, Cheltenham and Gloucester to the west, Stratford-upon-Avon to the north, and Bath to the south. This central position makes it accessible for day trips and longer stays from multiple major cities.

items.body: Key market towns include Cheltenham, Cirencester, Stow-on-the-Wold, Burford, Tewkesbury, Stroud, and Witney. These towns blend historic architecture with modern amenities, offering shopping, dining, and cultural events while retaining their traditional Cotswold character.

topic.title: Indonesian Archipelago: Key Facts
topic.summary: Fourteen concise, evidence‑based insights cover Indonesia’s language, geography, economy, culture and social practices, drawn exclusively from authoritative sources such as Wikipedia, Britannica and specialist guides.
topic.intro: Stretching across thousands of islands, Indonesia is the world’s largest archipelagic state. This guide presents fourteen distinct, verifiable claims about its national symbols, linguistic landscape, economic centre, ecological position and everyday customs, each backed by the supplied references.

items.title: National Motto
items.body: Indonesia’s national motto is “Bhinneka Tunggal Ika”, an Old Javanese phrase meaning “Unity in Diversity”. The motto appears on the state emblem and reflects the country’s official ideology of Pancasila, which promotes social harmony among its many ethnic and linguistic groups. This principle is highlighted in the Indonesian Wikipedia entry as a core element of national identity.

sources.title: Indonesia - Wikipedia

items.title: Official Language
items.body: The official language of Indonesia is Indonesian, a standardised form of Malay. It serves as the lingua franca for government, education and media nationwide. The language’s status is affirmed in both the English and Indonesian Wikipedia articles, which list Indonesian as the sole official language while acknowledging the existence of over seven hundred indigenous languages spoken across the archipelago.

sources.title: Indonesia - Wikipedia
Indonesia - Wikipedia bahasa Indonesia, ensiklopedia bebas

items.title: Capital City
items.body: Jakarta is both the capital and the largest city of Indonesia. Located on the northwest coast of Java, it functions as the political, economic and cultural centre of the nation. This detail is provided in the infobox of the English Wikipedia article, which lists Jakarta under “Capital and largest city” with its geographic coordinates.

sources.title: Indonesia - Wikipedia

items.title: Indigenous Language Count
items.body: Indonesia recognises 718 indigenous languages, reflecting its extraordinary linguistic diversity. This figure is cited in the English Wikipedia entry under “Indigenous languages”, noting the vast array of local tongues spoken alongside the national language. The count underscores the country’s status as one of the most multilingual nations on Earth.

sources.title: Indonesia - Wikipedia

items.title: Economic Profile
items.body: Indonesia possesses the largest economy in Southeast Asia, with services and industry contributing the majority of output. Economic activity is heavily concentrated on the island of Java, which hosts the nation’s main business hubs and industrial zones. This assessment appears in the English Wikipedia article, which links Indonesia’s economic strength to its regional dominance and geographic concentration.

sources.title: Indonesia - Wikipedia

items.title: Tectonic and Ecological Position
items.body: The Indonesian archipelago sits at a major juncture of Earth’s tectonic plates, spans two distinct faunal realms, and has historically acted as a cultural nexus between Oceania and mainland Asia. This description is supplied by the Britannica entry, which highlights the archipelago’s geological uniqueness and its long‑standing role in facilitating exchanges of peoples, flora and fauna across the region.

sources.title: Indonesia | History, Flag, Map, Capital, Language, Religion, & Facts ...

items.title: Lingua Franca Function
items.body: Bahasa Indonesia acts as a unifying lingua franca across Indonesia’s thousands of islands, enabling communication among speakers of over seven hundred local languages. The World Language Library notes that Indonesian connects the country’s diverse populations, serving as a vital tool for national cohesion and everyday interaction in both urban and rural settings.

sources.title: Learn Indonesian Online (Bahasa Indonesia)

items.title: Language Structure
items.body: Indonesian grammar is relatively simple: it lacks verb conjugations, gendered nouns and complex tenses. This structural simplicity makes the language accessible to learners and contributes to its role as a lingua franca. The World Language Library emphasises these features as key reasons why Indonesian is considered easy to acquire compared with many other Asian languages.

sources.title: Learn Indonesian Online (Bahasa Indonesia)

items.title: Vocabulary Influences
items.body: The Indonesian lexicon has absorbed loanwords from Dutch, Sanskrit, Arabic, Chinese, Portuguese and English, reflecting centuries of trade, colonisation and cultural contact. These influences are detailed in the World Language Library, which traces how historical interactions with European powers and Asian traders have enriched the language’s vocabulary.

sources.title: Learn Indonesian Online (Bahasa Indonesia)

items.title: Speaker Base
items.body: Approximately 270 million people speak Indonesian, including the vast majority of Indonesia’s population and expatriate communities in neighbouring Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore. The World Language Library provides this figure, noting that the language’s reach extends beyond national borders due to migration and regional ties.

sources.title: Learn Indonesian Online (Bahasa Indonesia)
